processing: Usually made as a Vietnamese pan-fired green tea: fresh shoots are heated to stop oxidation, rolled and dried. Exact methods vary by household and are not specific to the plant.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this plant in particular. As with other northern Vietnamese green teas, picking follows the warm growing season and young shoots are the prized part.
appearance_dry: Typical of Thai Nguyen green tea: small, dark green, tightly curled leaves.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear yellow-green, as with other Thai Nguyen green teas.
appearance_wet: Small, soft green leaves, in keeping with its small-leaf reputation.
taste_profile: Astringent at first and then sweet, with an aroma Vietnamese writers compare to com, young green rice.

brewing.notes: General guidance for Vietnamese green tea rather than a rule for this plant. Boiling water or a long steep brings the bitterness forward.

vintage_note: Trung Du is a plant, not a product with its own sale pattern, and its leaf is usually sold as Thai Nguyen or Tan Cuong green tea. As is usual for green tea, buy the most recent harvest and drink it fresh. Few packs name the plant, so ask the seller whether the leaf is Trung Du or a hybrid.
description:
Trung Du is the local small-leaf tea plant of Vietnam's northern midlands, and the name simply points to that region. It is a plant type rather than a finished tea, and around Thai Nguyen it is treated as the backbone of the Tan Cuong style.

Its leaf generally becomes pan-fired green tea, made as other Thai Nguyen greens are. What sets it apart is mostly the raw material, since hybrids now fill most of the fields. Reports put Trung Du at about a fifth of the tea area in the province and only about a tenth in Tan Cuong.

Vietnamese growers and writers describe a first wave of astringency that gives way to sweetness, with a young-rice aroma they say hybrids lack. Treat that as local opinion, and compare two cups side by side if you can. Water around 80°C keeps the bitterness in check, as with most green teas of the region.

The plant yields less than clonal cuttings and often sells for less, which is why many households hesitate to replant it. In return, it is said to hold its quality for decades. When buying, ask directly, because the label rarely tells you which plant you are getting.
history:
Little is documented about when Trung Du was first grown or named. It is regarded as a native plant of the northern midlands, with old stands surviving in Thai Nguyen.

Its recent story is one of decline and attempted rescue. Hybrids and clonal cuttings have replaced much of it because they crop more heavily, and local authorities in Thai Nguyen have funded efforts to preserve and replant it.
